title: Derivation of the General Solution of the Black-Scholes Boundary-Value Problem
abstract: There are infinitely many functions that satisfy the Black-Scholes partial differential equation and the terminal condition corresponding to the European call option. This means that the Black-Scholes formula, which led to the award of the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, is not the unique solution, as was once assumed. Consequently, it violates the law of one price, one of the fundamental laws of economics and finance. In this article, we present a rigorous derivation of these solutions to the Black-Scholes boundary value problem.
summary: This paper mathematically proves that the standard Black-Scholes formula for option pricing is not the unique solution to the governing partial differential equation. By transforming the problem into a heat-equation form, the authors derive a general solution that includes the standard formula as a specific instance, thereby challenging a fundamental assumption in financial theory.
main_problem: To rigorously derive the general solution to the Black-Scholes Boundary-Value Problem (BVP) for European option pricing.
main_result: The Black-Scholes formula is not the unique solution to the BVP, implying a violation of the law of one price. A general solution $w_\zeta(x_t, t)$ is derived that encompasses the standard formula as a special case.
method: The problem is transformed into solving a partial differential equation (PDE) that reduces to the Kolmogorov-Fokker-Planck equation, solved using Green's function techniques and properties of Hermite polynomials.
model_or_system: The model is the Black-Scholes framework for option pricing, governed by a specific PDE and a terminal condition related to the option payoff. The mathematical analysis involves transforming variables to simplify the PDE into a heat-equation form.
key_observables: The general solution $w_\zeta(x_t, t)$, the standard Black-Scholes price $w_{BS}(x_t, t)$, and the derived put option price $p_\zeta(x_t, t)$.
important_parameters: The time to maturity $	au = T-t$, the interest rate $r$, and the volatility $v$.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on established properties of Hermite polynomials and involves taking limits ($	au 	o 0$) to complete the solution.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the BVP and the non-uniqueness of the solution. It then uses change of variables to map the PDE to the Kolmogorov-Fokker-Planck equation. The core of the work involves deriving explicit components ($I_l, J_l, B_l$) using Hermite polynomial properties, culminating in the general solution structure.
why_interesting: While the subject is finance, the mathematical machinery—solving a parabolic PDE (heat equation) with specific boundary/terminal conditions using advanced techniques like Green's functions and orthogonal polynomials—is highly relevant to open quantum systems and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
